# Crank--Nicolson Method

## Biological problem

We consider a substance with concentration $u(x,t)$ that diffuses in one spatial dimension with a constant diffusion coefficient $D$. Point-like agents that act as sources and sinks in this one dimensional space, they may secrete the substance into the environment or remove it through uptake. These point-like agents might represent individual bacterium or discrete protein clusters positioned at specific locations along a filament or channel.

:::{.callout-note title="Dimensions and units"}

We use the following dimensions and units:

- $M$ denotes 'amount of substance' (e.g. units of moles, molecules, or mass).
- $L$ denotes the length (e.g. µm), 
- $T$ denotes time (e.g. seconds).

Where dimension-generic expressions are given, $d$ denotes the number of spatial dimensions. For this document $d=1$.
:::

 

## Equation to solve

The governing diffusion--reaction equation is

$$
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}
=
D \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2}
+
O(x)
-
I(x,u,t).
$$ {#eq-diffusion-source-sink}

Here,

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|---|---|---|
| $u(x,t)$ | Extracellular concentration | $M/L^d$ |
| $\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2}$ | Second spatial derivative | $M/L^{d+2}$ |
| $D$ | Diffusion coefficient | $L^2/T$ |
| $O(x)$ | Source term (production of $u$) | $M/(L^d\,T)$ |
| $I(x,u,t)$ | Sink term (uptake of $u$) | $M/(L^d\,T)$ |


## Point-like sources and sinks

Let $B_o$ denote the set of secreting agents and $B_i$ the set of consuming agents. Let $x_s$ be the position of agent $s$.

The agents are represented as point-like sources and sinks using Dirac delta functions

$$
O(x)
=
K_O
\sum_{s\in B_o}
\delta(x-x_s), 
$$

$$
I(x,u,t)
=
K_I\,u(x,t)
\sum_{s\in B_i}
\delta(x-x_s).
$$
$K_O$ is the **per-agent secretion rate** or **point-source strength**. It specifies the amount of substance secreted by one agent per unit time. All secreting agents are assumed to have the same $K_O$, with units of $M/T$. This is an intrinsic bacterial property independent of the geometry of space.

$K_I$ is the **per-agent first-order uptake coefficient**. The uptake rate of a consuming agent is proportional to the local extracellular concentration. All consuming agents are assumed to have the same $K_I$. Unlike $K_O$, the units of $K_I$ depend on the spatial dimension $d$: $K_I$ carries units of $L^d / T$, because the Dirac delta function $\delta(x)$ has units of $1/L^d$ and the sink term $I = K_I\, u\, \delta$ must have units of $M/(L^d\, T)$. In one spatial dimension $(d=1)$, $K_I$ therefore has units of $L/T$.

```{.typescript #define-time-stepping-logic filename="define-time-stepping-logic"}
            const u_im1: number = uCurrent[N - 2];
            const u_i: number   = uCurrent[N - 1];
            const u_ip1: number = uCurrent[N - 2];   // ghost cell: u_n = u_{n-2}

            const rhsVal: number =

                (1.0 - 2.0 * lambda - beta[i]) * u_i +
                lambda * u_ip1 +
                q[i];

            d[i] = rhsVal;

        thomasAlgorithm(
            lowerDiagonal,
            mainDiagonal,
            upperDiagonal,
            d,
            N,
            modifiedUpper,
            modifiedRHS,
            solution,
        );

        let hasNegative: boolean = false;
        for (let i: number = 0; i < N; i++) {
            uNext[i] = solution[i];
            if (!allowNegativeValues && uNext[i] < 0) {
                hasNegative = true;
            }
        }

        if (hasNegative && !allowNegativeValues) {
            throw new Error(
                "Negative concentrations encountered in CNTimeStepping step " + step,
            );
        }

        const tmp: Float64Array = uCurrent;
        uCurrent = uNext;
        uNext = tmp;
    }

    for (let i: number = 0; i < N; i++) {
        concentrationData[i] = uCurrent[i];
    }
```

```{ojs}
//|code-fold: true
d3 = require("d3@7")

N = 6 // number of grid points, indices 0..5

  schematic = {
    const width = 420, height = 240;
    const marginX = 60;

    const displayItems = (() => {
      if (N <= 5) {
        return d3.range(N).map(i => {
          const item = { type: "node", i, x: i };
          if (i === N - 2) item.indexLabel = "N-2";
          else if (i === N - 1) item.indexLabel = "N-1";
          else item.indexLabel = String(i);
          return item;
        });
      }
      return [
        { type: "node", i: 0, x: 0, indexLabel: "0" },
        { type: "node", i: 1, x: 1, indexLabel: "1" },
        { type: "node", i: 2, x: 2, indexLabel: "2" },
        { type: "dots" },
        { type: "node", i: N - 2, x: N - 2, indexLabel: "N-2" },
        { type: "node", i: N - 1, x: N - 1, indexLabel: "N-1" }
      ];
    })();

  const nodeItems = displayItems.filter(d => d.type === "node");

  const yN  = 90;  // baseline for time level n
  const yN1 = 190; // baseline for time level n+1

  const x = d3.scaleLinear()
      .domain([0, N - 1])
      .range([marginX, width - marginX]);

  const svg = d3.create("svg")
      .attr("width", width)
      .attr("height", height);

  svg.append("defs").append("marker")
      .attr("id", "arrow")

      .attr("fill", "gray");

  function drawRow(y, label) {
    const safeId = label.replace("+", "");

    svg.append("line")
        .attr("x1", x(0)).attr("x2", x(N - 1))
        .attr("y1", y).attr("y2", y)
        .attr("stroke", "black")
        .attr("stroke-width", 1.5);

    svg.selectAll(`circle.row-${safeId}`)
      .data(nodeItems)
      .join("circle")
        .attr("class", `row-${safeId}`)
        .attr("cx", d => x(d.x))
        .attr("cy", y)
        .attr("r", 6)
        .attr("fill", "grey");

    svg.append("text")
        .attr("x", marginX - 25)
        .attr("y", y + 4)
        .attr("text-anchor", "middle")
        .attr("font-weight", "bold")
        .text(label);
  }
  drawRow(yN, "n");
  drawRow(yN1, "n+1");

  displayItems.forEach(d => {
    if (d.type === "node") {
      svg.append("text")
        .attr("x", x(d.x))
        .attr("y", yN - 22)
        .attr("text-anchor", "middle")
        .attr("font-size", "14px")
        .text(d.indexLabel);
    } else {
      svg.append("text")
        .attr("x", (x(2) + x(N - 2)) / 2)
        .attr("y", yN - 22)
        .attr("text-anchor", "middle")
        .attr("font-size", "12px")
        .text("…");
    }
  });

  nodeItems.forEach(d => {
    svg.append("line")
        .attr("x1", x(d.x)).attr("x2", x(d.x))
        .attr("y1", yN + 6).attr("y2", yN1 - 6)
        .attr("stroke", "lightgray")
        .attr("stroke-dasharray", "3,3");
  });

  svg.append("line")
      .attr("x1", marginX - 25).attr("x2", marginX - 25)
      .attr("y1", yN + 15).attr("y2", yN1 - 15)
      .attr("stroke", "gray")
      .attr("marker-end", "url(#arrow)")
      .attr("marker-start", "url(#arrow)");

  svg.append("text")
      .attr("x", marginX - 45)
      .attr("y", (yN + yN1) / 2 + 4)
      .attr("text-anchor", "middle")
      .text("Δt");

  svg.append("line")
      .attr("x1", x(0)+12).attr("x2", x(1)-12)
      .attr("y1", yN - 25).attr("y2", yN - 25)
      .attr("stroke", "gray")
      .attr("marker-end", "url(#arrow)")
      .attr("marker-start", "url(#arrow)");

  svg.append("text")
      .attr("x", (x(0) + x(1)) / 2)
      .attr("y", yN - 32)
      .attr("text-anchor", "middle")
      .text("Δx");

  svg.append("text")
      .attr("x", width / 2)
      .attr("y", 15)   // was 20
      .attr("text-anchor", "middle")
      .attr("font-weight", "bold")
      .text("Crank–Nicolson space–time grid");

  const container = document.createElement("div");
  container.style.textAlign = "center";
  container.appendChild(svg.node());
  return container;
}
```


The domain is discretized on a uniform grid of `N` ($N$) points with spacing `dx` ($\Delta x$) and time step `dt` ($\Delta t$). The arrays `uCurrent` and `uNext` store the concentration at the current and next time steps, respectively. `uCurrent`
stores $u_i^n$, which approximates $u(x_i, t^n)$, and `uNext` stores $u_i^{n+1}$, which approximates $u(x_i, t^{n+1})$. These variables and arrays are defined at module scope as

### Variable declaration

 These variables are declared in `define-module-globals`

```{.typescript #declare-grid-params-u filename="declare-grid-params-u"}
let N: number;
let dx: number;
let dt: number;
let uCurrent: Float64Array;
let uNext: Float64Array;
```

### Variable initialization 

The parameters values are initialized
in `CNSetup` from its parameters `length`, `deltaX`, and `deltaT`)


```{.typescript #assign-grid-params filename="assign-grid-params" }
N = length;
dx = deltaX;
dt = deltaT;
```
and the arrays are allocated in `CNSetup` using the grid size `N`.

```{.typescript #alloc-u filename="alloc-u"}
if (!uCurrent) uCurrent = new Float64Array(N);
if (!uNext) uNext = new Float64Array(N);
```



which `CNTimeStepping` can then use during time stepping.









## Discretization of the Laplacian and Source/Sink Terms


The Laplacian is discretized as follows

$$
\nabla^2(u_i^n)
=
\frac{u_{i-1}^n - 2u_i^n + u_{i+1}^n}{\Delta x^2}.
$$ {#eq-laplacian}


Let $m_i^{(O)}$ and $m_i^{(I)}$ denote the number of secreting and consuming agents in grid cell $i$, and let $i_s$ be the grid index of the cell to which agent $s$ is assigned (for example, the nearest grid cell). Then

$$
m_i^{(O)} = \sum_{s\in B_o} \delta_{i,i_s}, \qquad
m_i^{(I)} = \sum_{s\in B_i} \delta_{i,i_s},
$$ {#eq-agents-counts}
Here,  $\delta_{i,i_s}$ is the Kronecker delta, which is dimensionless (unlike the Dirac delta $\delta(x)$ used in the continuous case, which has units of $1/L^d$).

Then, the source and sink terms can be discretized as

$$
O_i
=
\frac{K_O}{\Delta x}
m_i^{(O)}
$$ {#eq-source-discrete}


$$
I_i^n
=
\frac{K_I}{\Delta x}
u_i^n
m_i^{(I)}
$$ {#eq-sink-discrete}

The factor $1/\Delta x$ represents each point-like agent as a source or sink distributed over its assigned grid cell. Consequently, integrating the discrete source or sink over that cell recovers the secretion or uptake associated with that agent. 

## Crank--Nicolson scheme 

Using the Crank--Nicolson method, the diffusion and uptake terms are averaged between time levels $n$ and $n+1$. Since the secretion term is assumed constant in time, it is included directly:

$$
\frac{u_i^{n+1} - u_i^n}{\Delta t}
=
\frac{D}{2}
\left[
\nabla^2(u_i^{n+1}) + \nabla^2(u_i^n)
\right]
+
O_i
-
\frac{1}{2}
\left[
I_i^{n+1} + I_i^n
\right].
$${#eq-crank-nicolson}

Inserting the explicit forms of the discrete Laplacian, source term and sink term (@eq-laplacian, @eq-source-discrete, @eq-sink-discrete) into
@eq-crank-nicolson and multiplying by $\Delta t$, we arrive at the linear system


$$
\begin{aligned}
u_i^{n+1} - u_i^n
={}&
\frac{D \Delta t}{2 \Delta x^2}
\Bigl[
    u_{i-1}^{n+1}
    - 2u_i^{n+1}
    + u_{i+1}^{n+1}
    + u_{i-1}^{n}
    - 2u_i^{n}
    + u_{i+1}^{n}
\Bigr]
\\
&+
\frac{K_O \Delta t}{\Delta x}
m_i^{(O)}
\\
&-
\frac{K_I \Delta t}{2\Delta x}
m_i^{(I)}
\Bigl[
    u_i^n + u_i^{n+1}
\Bigr]
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-crank-nicolson-expanded}


For convenience, define the parameters $\lambda$ , $q_i$, and $\beta_i$:

$$
\lambda
=
\frac{D \Delta t}{2\Delta x^2}
\qquad
q_i=
\frac{K_O \Delta t}{\Delta x}m_i^{(O)},
\qquad
\beta_i
=
\frac{K_I \Delta t}{2\Delta x}m_i^{(I)}
$$

### Parameter declaration

$\lambda$, $q$, and $\beta$ are declared in `define-module-globals`

```{.typescript #declare-lambda-q-beta filename="declare-lambda-q-beta"}
let lambda: number;  
let q: Float64Array;
let beta: Float64Array;
```

### Parameter initialization

Lambda is computed in `CNSetup` as

```{.typescript #compute-lambda filename="compute-lambda"}
lambda = (D * dt) / (2.0 * dx * dx);
```

and the arrays `q` and `beta` are allocated with size `N` in `CNSetup` as well 

```{.typescript #alloc-q-beta filename="alloc-q-beta"}
if (!q) q = new Float64Array(N);
if (!beta) beta = new Float64Array(N);
```

and filled using the formulas for $q_i$ and $\beta_i$ derived above.

```{.typescript #fill-q-beta filename="fill-q-beta"}
for (let i: number = 0; i < N; i++) {
	q[i] = (K_O * dt) / dx * sourceCounts[i];
	beta[i] = (K_I * dt) / (2.0 * dx) * sinkCounts[i];
}
```

where `D`, `K_O`, and `K_I` are coefficients passed as a parameter to `CNSetup`; and `sourceCounts` and `sinkCounts` are arrays of length `N` passed as parameters to `CNSetup` containing $m_i^{(O)}$ and $m_i^{(I)}$, respectively.


## Tridiagonal system

Then @eq-crank-nicolson-expanded can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}
u_i^{n+1} - u_i^n
={}&
\lambda
\Bigl[
    u_{i-1}^{n+1}
    - 2u_i^{n+1}
    + u_{i+1}^{n+1}
    + u_{i-1}^{n}
    - 2u_i^{n}
    + u_{i+1}^{n}
\Bigr]
\\
&+
q_i
-
\beta_i
\Bigl[
    u_i^n + u_i^{n+1}
\Bigr].
\end{aligned}
$$

Collecting the unknown terms at time level $n+1$ on the left-hand side gives

$$
- \lambda u_{i-1}^{n+1}
+ \left(1 + 2\lambda + \beta_i\right) u_i^{n+1}
- \lambda u_{i+1}^{n+1}
=
 \lambda u_{i-1}^{n}
+\left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_i\right) u_i^n
+\lambda u_{i+1}^{n}
+q_i.
$$ {#eq-crank-nicolson-tridiagonal}

This equation applies to every grid point $i=0,\ldots,N-1$, so that for a spatial domain with $N$ grid points, we obtain a system of $N$ linear equations. For a case with Neuman boundary conditions, the system can be written in matrix form as $A u^{n+1} = d$, where $A$ is the $N \times N$ tridiagonal matrix

$$
A =
\begin{bmatrix}
1 + 2\lambda + \beta_0 & -2\lambda & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
-\lambda & 1 + 2\lambda + \beta_1 & -\lambda & \ddots & \vdots \\
0 & -\lambda & \ddots & \ddots & 0 \\
\vdots & \ddots & \ddots & 1 + 2\lambda + \beta_{N-2} & -\lambda \\
0 & \cdots & 0 & -2\lambda & 1 + 2\lambda + \beta_{N-1}
\end{bmatrix},
$$

$u^{n+1}$ is the unknown vector of concentrations at time level $n+1$,

$$
u^{n+1} =
\begin{bmatrix}
u_0^{n+1} \\
u_1^{n+1} \\
\vdots \\
u_{N-2}^{n+1} \\
u_{N-1}^{n+1}
\end{bmatrix},
$$

and the right-hand side vector $d$ is given by

$$
d =
\begin{bmatrix}
\left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_0\right) u_0^n + 2\lambda u_1^n + q_0 \\
\lambda u_0^n + \left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_1\right) u_1^n + \lambda u_2^n + q_1 \\
\vdots \\
\lambda u_{N-3}^n + \left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_{N-2}\right) u_{N-2}^n + \lambda u_{N-1}^n + q_{N-2} \\
2\lambda u_{N-2}^n + \left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_{N-1}\right) u_{N-1}^n + q_{N-1}
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Here, the entries of $A$ and $d$ at the boundaries $i=0$ and $i=N-1$ incorporate Neumann (zero-flux) boundary conditions.



:::{.callout-note collapse=true title='Example for $N=5$ and Neuman BC'}

If we apply this equation to $5$ grid points ($i=0,1,2,3,4$), we obtain a system of $5$ linear equations for the unknowns $u_i^{n+1}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}
-{\color{red} \lambda u_{-1}^{n+1}}
+ \left(1 + 2\lambda + \beta_0\right) u_0^{n+1}
- \lambda u_{1}^{n+1}
={}&
{\color{red} \lambda u_{-1}^{n}}
+\left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_0\right) u_0^n
+\lambda u_{1}^{n}
+q_0,
\\
- \lambda u_{0}^{n+1}
+ \left(1 + 2\lambda + \beta_1\right) u_1^{n+1}
- \lambda u_{2}^{n+1}
={}&
 \lambda u_{0}^{n}
+\left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_1\right) u_1^n
+\lambda u_{2}^{n}
+q_1,
\\
- \lambda u_{1}^{n+1}
+ \left(1 + 2\lambda + \beta_2\right) u_2^{n+1}
- \lambda u_{3}^{n+1}
={}&
 \lambda u_{1}^{n}
+\left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_2\right) u_2^n
+\lambda u_{3}^{n}
+q_2,
\\
- \lambda u_{2}^{n+1}
+ \left(1 + 2\lambda + \beta_3\right) u_3^{n+1}
 - \lambda u_{4}^{n+1}
={}&
 \lambda u_{2}^{n}
+\left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_3\right) u_3^n
+\lambda u_{4}^{n}
+q_3,
\\
 - \lambda u_{3}^{n+1}
+ \left(1 + 2\lambda + \beta_4\right) u_4^{n+1}
 - {\color{red} \lambda u_{5}^{n+1}}
={}&
 \lambda u_{3}^{n}
+\left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_4\right) u_4^n
+{\color{red}\lambda u_{5}^{n}}
+q_4.
\end{aligned}
$$
Here, the red terms correspond to cells outside the domain which represent the boundary conditions. These are set to a constant value in the case of Dirichlet boundary conditions, or set via centered difference mirroring in the case of Neumann (zero-flux) boundary conditions. For this implementation, we use Neumann zero-flux boundary conditions. With centered differences, zero flux at the left boundary implies $u_{-1} = u_1$, and at the right boundary $u_{N} = u_{N-2}$. This way, by setting $u_{-1} = u_1$ and $u_5 = u_3$, we can eliminate the red terms, giving 

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left(1 + 2\lambda + \beta_0\right) u_0^{n+1} - 2\lambda u_{1}^{n+1}
={}&
\left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_0\right) u_0^n
+ 2\lambda u_{1}^{n}
+q_0,
\\
- \lambda u_{0}^{n+1}
+ \left(1 + 2\lambda + \beta_1\right) u_1^{n+1}
- \lambda u_{2}^{n+1}
={}&
 \lambda u_{0}^{n}
+\left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_1\right) u_1^n
+\lambda u_{2}^{n}
+q_1,
\\
- \lambda u_{1}^{n+1}
+ \left(1 + 2\lambda + \beta_2\right) u_2^{n+1}
- \lambda u_{3}^{n+1}
={}&
 \lambda u_{1}^{n}
+\left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_2\right) u_2^n
+\lambda u_{3}^{n}
+q_2,
\\
- \lambda u_{2}^{n+1}
+ \left(1 + 2\lambda + \beta_3\right) u_3^{n+1}
- \lambda u_{4}^{n+1}
={}&
 \lambda u_{2}^{n}
+\left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_3\right) u_3^n
+\lambda u_{4}^{n}
+q_3,
\\
- 2\lambda u_{3}^{n+1}
+ \left(1 + 2\lambda + \beta_4\right) u_4^{n+1}
={}&
 2\lambda u_{3}^{n}
+\left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_4\right) u_4^n
+q_4.
\end{aligned}
$$

This is a tridiagonal system that can be represented in matrix form as $A u^{n+1} = d$, where $A$ is

$$
A =
\begin{bmatrix}
1 + 2\lambda + \beta_0 & -2\lambda & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
-\lambda & 1 + 2\lambda + \beta_1 & -\lambda & 0 & 0 \\
0 & -\lambda & 1 + 2\lambda + \beta_2 & -\lambda & 0 \\
0 & 0 & -\lambda & 1 + 2\lambda + \beta_3 & -\lambda \\
0 & 0 & 0 & -2\lambda & 1 + 2\lambda + \beta_4
\end{bmatrix},
$$

$u^{n+1}$ is

$$
u^{n+1} =
\begin{bmatrix}
u_0^{n+1} \\
u_1^{n+1} \\
u_2^{n+1} \\
u_3^{n+1} \\
u_4^{n+1}
\end{bmatrix}
$$

and the right-hand side vector $d$ is
$$
d =
\begin{bmatrix}
\left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_0\right) u_0^n + 2\lambda u_1^n + q_0 \\
\lambda u_0^n + \left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_1\right) u_1^n + \lambda u_2^n + q_1 \\
\lambda u_1^n + \left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_2\right) u_2^n + \lambda u_3^n + q_2 \\
\lambda u_2^n + \left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_3\right) u_3^n + \lambda u_4^n + q_3 \\
2\lambda u_3^n + \left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_4\right) u_4^n + q_4
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

:::


The solution vector $u^{n+1}$ is solved from the system $A u^{n+1} = d$ using the Thomas algorithm, which implementation lives in a separate module. 


### Diagonals declaration

The matrix $A$ is built from the lower, main, and upper diagonals, which are declared in `define-module-globals` as

```{.typescript #declare-diagonals filename="declare-diagonals"}
let lowerDiagonal: Float64Array;
let mainDiagonal: Float64Array;
let upperDiagonal: Float64Array;
```

### Diagonals initialization

The diagonals are then initialized in `CNSetup` as

```{.typescript #alloc-diagonals filename="alloc-diagonals"}
if (!lowerDiagonal) lowerDiagonal = new Float64Array(N);
if (!mainDiagonal) mainDiagonal = new Float64Array(N);
if (!upperDiagonal) upperDiagonal = new Float64Array(N);
```

and then filled with their corresponding parameters

```{.typescript #fill-diagonals filename="fill-diagonals"}
    for (let i: number = 1; i < N - 1; i++) {
        lowerDiagonal[i] = -lambda;
        mainDiagonal[i] = 1.0 + 2.0 * lambda + beta[i];
        upperDiagonal[i] = -lambda;
    }

    lowerDiagonal[0] = 0.0;
    mainDiagonal[0] = 1.0 + 2.0 * lambda + beta[0];
    upperDiagonal[0] = -2.0 * lambda;

    lowerDiagonal[N - 1] = -2.0 * lambda;
    mainDiagonal[N - 1] = 1.0 + 2.0 * lambda + beta[N - 1];
    upperDiagonal[N - 1] = 0.0;

```


## Thomas‑solver scratch arrays

The Thomas algorithm is a **destructive** solver: during forward elimination it overwrites the upper diagonal and right‑hand side, and during backward substitution it writes the solution into yet another array. If `thomasAlgorithm` allocated these three arrays internally on every call, the time‑stepping loop — which may run hundreds of thousands of iterations — would stress the garbage collector and degrade performance. Instead, the three arrays are pre‑allocated once in `CNSetup` and held at module scope so that the solver runs with **zero per‑step allocation**.

A second benefit is that the original matrix diagonals (`lowerDiagonal`, `mainDiagonal`, `upperDiagonal`) remain untouched. They describe the stationary structure of the tridiagonal system and can be reused across every time step. The scratch arrays isolate the destructive elimination phase from that structural description; only when the source/sink configuration changes (`rebuildMatrix = true`) do the diagonals themselves need recomputation.

| Array | Role | Contents after forward sweep |
|---|---|---|
| `modifiedUpper` | Transformed upper diagonal | `c′₀, c′₁, …, c′ₙ₋₂` |
| `modifiedRHS` | Transformed right‑hand side | `d′₀, d′₁, …, d′ₙ₋₁` |
| `solution` | Final concentration at time `n+1` | `u₀ⁿ⁺¹, u₁ⁿ⁺¹, …, uₙ₋₁ⁿ⁺¹` |


They are declared at `define-module-globals` as

```{.typescript #declare-thomas-scratch-arrays filename="declare-thomas-scratch-arrays"}
let modifiedUpper: Float64Array;
let modifiedRHS: Float64Array;
let solution: Float64Array;
```

and reallocated in `CNSetup` as

```{.typescript #alloc-thomas-scratch-arrays filename="alloc-thomas-scratch-arrays"}
if (!modifiedUpper) modifiedUpper = new Float64Array(N);
if (!modifiedRHS) modifiedRHS = new Float64Array(N);
if (!solution) solution = new Float64Array(N);
```


## Module‑level state

```{.typescript #define-module-vars filename="define-module-vars"}

<<declare-diagonals>>
<<declare-thomas-scratch-arrays>>
```

## Setting up the Crank‑Nicolson coefficients

`CNSetup` must be called once before any simulation. It stores
the grid length and computes the coefficients that define the
tridiagonal system. Neumann (zero‑flux) boundary conditions are
implemented by adjusting the first and last rows of the matrix using
ghost‑cell mirroring.



## The time‑stepping loop

The main `CNTimeStepping` function advances the concentration field by
`totalNumberOfIterations` time steps. At each step it builds the
right‑hand side vector using the explicit part of the scheme (including
source terms and Neumann boundary conditions via ghost‑cell mirroring),
solves the tridiagonal system with the Thomas algorithm, and then swaps
the solution arrays for the next iteration.

If a negative concentration appears and `allowNegativeValues` is
`false`, the function throws an error.


## Assembling the module

The final code block tells Entangled to write the file
`src/crankNicolson.js` by concatenating all the pieces defined above.
